summary:
Bangladesh's Penal Code of 1860, Section 377 ("Unnatural offences"), punishes voluntary "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment of either description for a term that may extend to ten years, and a fine. The explanation attached to the section treats penetration as sufficient and extends its ambit to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual acts. The provision entered the territory's law through the British Indian Penal Code of 1860, was carried into the Pakistan Penal Code after the 1947 partition and retained at independence in 1971, and Parliament declined to repeal it in 2009 and again in 2013.

Whether Section 377 reaches sexual conduct between women is unresolved. A UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (September 2023, updated April 2026) records the ambiguity: ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere describing the provision as relevant to all genders.

Outright International, in material updated 12 March 2026, describes prosecution under the section as rare but records police use of it to harass people presumed LGBTIQ. LGBTI groups report the section used as a pretext to bully individuals considered effeminate and to limit registration of LGBTI organisations, alongside harassment under a "suspicious behaviour" provision of the police code. In May 2017 Rapid Action Battalion forces raided the Chayaneer Community Center in Keraniganj Upazila during an LGBTI dinner, separated about 120 people into small groups, beat them and arrested 28 on suspicion of homosexual activity while allowing media to photograph some; authorities later characterised the arrests as narcotics possession, with four remanded, 12 detained for questioning and 12 sent directly to jail.

Documented police violence against visibly trans people in 2025 is extortion-driven. After hijras refused a police extortion payment on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack at Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 September 2025 police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates in Narayanganj, a traditional livelihood. In April 2024 five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, which places documented policing of visibly trans people at a principal transit hub.

Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district and widely known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025; five unidentified individuals were accused. JMBF's annual report, cited on 7 April 2026, records 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025, described as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend since 2022, covering murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Conditions shifted after the August 2024 ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Reporting on 5 August 2025 described Bangladesh's LGBTQ community as increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats a year after the government fell. Global Press Journal reported that hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, that third-gender identity has been officially recognised since 2013, and that the featured trans subject now lives in hiding. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019 (PA/07096/2017) recorded Home Office country material describing Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.

On documents and status, the cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina recognised hijra as a separate gender alongside male and female for identification on official documents on 11 November 2013, with a Ministry of Social Welfare survey counting approximately 10,000 registered hijras who were already enlisted as voters. Voter lists offer a third-gender option, hijra candidates have run for government positions, and in April 2019 officials introduced "hijra" as a third-gender option on voting forms. Gender-marker change is permitted. The country has no policy setting out measures an individual must undergo to change gender legally on official documents, no stated criteria for who qualifies as hijra, and transgender communities beyond the hijra category remain unrecognised and unprotected from discrimination.

Recognition has not produced legal protection. There is no protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, and the law recognises no same-sex relationship, civil union, domestic partnership or adoption route for such couples; same-sex couples have been detained and can be imprisoned or fined. On 17 April 2022 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that treating LGBT rights and same-sex marriage as human rights is a regrettable and uncalled-for imposition of values from a select few countries, in response to the US Bangladesh 2021 Human Rights Report released on 13 April 2022. Alongside this, third-gender identity has been officially recognised since 2013, a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021, and LGBTIQ and hijra pride events have been held.
tangentialFactors:
The education sector has produced dated incidents of exclusion. In November 2023 transgender woman Hochemin Islam faced exclusion from the North South University women's carnival on security grounds amid student threats of unrest, an exam boycott and rally banners explicitly reading "no transgender". On 19 January 2024 part-time BRAC University lecturer Asif Mahtab Utsha publicly tore the seventh-grade History and Social Science textbook story "Sharifar Golpo", in which a character born male later identifies as a woman living as a hijra, prompting student protests with "Say No To LGBTQ" banners and class boycott calls, his removal from lectures, and a five-member Education Ministry review that four months later found nineteen words "incompatible" with Bangladeshi society and recommended their omission. In August 2025 transgender woman Sahara Chowdhury, a final-year English student at Metropolitan University in Sylhet, was expelled for life on stated grounds of online threats and carrying a weapon causing fear, which she denied, following her sharing of a satirical caricature.

The 2017 US Department of State human rights report described the transgender population as long marginalised but recognised, facing "continued high levels of fear, harassment, and law enforcement contact" in the wake of violent extremist attacks against vulnerable communities, and recorded LGBTI members receiving threatening messages by telephone, text and social media with some harassed by police. It also recorded that after the 2017 raid and continued harassment, many members including leadership reduced activities and sought refuge inside and outside the country, severely weakening advocacy and support networks.

The incident figures carried here are raw counts of documented cases. The 260 violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals in 2025 are nationwide documented incidents with no population denominator, and the population counted is LGBTQI+ broadly rather than trans people alone, so the figure indicates a documented trend since 2022 rather than a per-capita rate of risk.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing measures sit beside the discrimination. In December 2014 the Ministry of Social Welfare invited hijras to apply for government employment, and in July 2015, after a hijra witnessed the murder of a secular blogger and helped arrest the perpetrators, the government announced plans to recruit and enlist hijras as traffic police. A government housing scheme for homeless or landless individuals included transgender people for the first time, with at least 140 transgender community members provided government-built houses across the country, and Bangladesh opened its first religious school for transgender people in Dhaka with classes starting 7 November 2020 for more than 150 expected students in Islamic and vocational subjects, free of charge and with no age limit.

In January 2015 the Ministry of Health issued a memorandum requesting necessary steps to identify hijras by conducting thorough medical check-ups requiring them to strip and have their genitals confirmed, with photographs later released to confirm that hijras are "really men".

Labour law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but does not prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, social status or caste, and there are no legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation. LGBTI organisations report police use of Section 377 to limit their registration. Organisations specifically assisting lesbians are rare, and social stigma against HIV and AIDS and against higher-risk populations is recorded as a barrier to accessing health services, especially for the transgender community and men who have sex with men. Despite historically held culturally important roles and greater general acceptance, hijras continue to face severe discrimination and unequal access to housing and health care.
outOfScopeNotes:
The record contains no sourced information on entry or visa rules, border document checks, or screening procedures that could expose a visitor's gender identity or trans status; no treatment differential to trans travellers at immigration is documented here.

Not sourced: bathroom and facilities rules, access to gender-affirming care for visitors, and any hate-crime provision covering anti-trans violence or its enforcement.

Unresolved: whether Section 377 applies to sexual conduct between women; whether the January 2015 medical-verification memorandum remains in force and what procedure currently governs gender-marker change in practice; whether the July 2015 plan to recruit hijras as traffic police proceeded; and whether charges were pursued after the May 2017 Keraniganj raid. The JMBF count for 2025 gives no denominator and covers LGBTQI+ people broadly rather than trans people alone.
